Make Disciples
mayk dih-SY-pulz
verb phrase (biblical command)
The single Greek imperative mathēteusate ("make disciples," "disciple") at the heart of the Great Commission (Matthew 28:19). It is the only finite verb of command in the commission; "go," "baptizing," and "teaching" are participles that modify it. From mathētēs, a learner or apprentice.

📖 Biblical Definition

"Make disciples" is the central command of the Great Commission and, grammatically, the only imperative in it: "Go ye therefore, and teach [make disciples of] all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost: Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you" (Matt 28:19-20). In the Greek, the one finite imperative is mathēteusate (make disciples); the surrounding words — going, baptizing, teaching — are participles that describe how the disciple-making is carried out. This grammar matters: the church's commission is not first to go, nor first to baptize, nor first to teach, but to MAKE DISCIPLES, with going, baptizing, and teaching as the means. A disciple (mathētēs) is a learner-apprentice who follows a master, takes his yoke, and is conformed to his life and teaching (Matt 11:29; Luke 6:40, "every one that is perfect shall be as his master"). Disciple-making therefore is not mere decision-eliciting or crowd-gathering; it is the patient formation of apprentices who are baptized into the Triune name and taught to observe all that Christ commanded. The two participles mark the two halves: baptism (the initiatory mark of covenant membership) and teaching-to-observe (the lifelong formation in obedience). From the Reformed standpoint, disciple-making is the ordinary work of the local church through the ordained means of grace, and its scope is all nations — the command is universal in reach and comprehensive in depth ("all things whatsoever I have commanded").

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The central command of the Great Commission and its only imperative (Greek mathēteusate, Matt 28:19); going, baptizing, and teaching are the participial means; disciple-making is the patient formation of baptized apprentices taught to observe all Christ commanded.

MAKE DISCIPLES, verb phrase. Greek mathēteusate (Matthew 28:19), the only imperative in the Great Commission.

Going, baptizing, and teaching are participles describing how the disciple-making is carried out.

A disciple (mathētēs) is a learner-apprentice conformed to his master's life and teaching (Luke 6:40).

Two participial halves: baptism (initiatory covenant mark) and teaching-to-observe (lifelong formation in obedience). Scope: all nations.

📖 Key Scripture

Matthew 28:19-20 — "Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost: Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you: and, lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world. Amen."

Luke 6:40 — "The disciple is not above his master: but every one that is perfect shall be as his master."

Matthew 11:29 — "Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls."

Acts 14:21 — "And when they had preached the gospel to that city, and had taught many, they returned again to Lystra, and to Iconium, and Antioch."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Make disciples is corrupted when reduced to decision-eliciting or crowd-gathering that stops at conversion, when the going is elevated above the disciple-making it merely modifies, or when the "teaching to observe all things" is trimmed to a comfortable subset of Christ's commands.

expand to see more

Decision-over-discipleship misreading. Much modern evangelism treats the commission as fulfilled when a decision is secured — a hand raised, a prayer prayed, a card signed. But the imperative is make DISCIPLES, not make decisions; and a disciple is an apprentice formed over time, baptized into the covenant and taught to observe all Christ commanded. Decisional evangelism that gathers crowds and elicits professions without forming obedient apprentices has done the participle (a kind of going and proclaiming) while neglecting the imperative (making disciples). The Lord did not commission us to produce converts but to produce disciples.

Trimmed-teaching misreading. The commission specifies "teaching them to observe ALL THINGS whatsoever I have commanded you" (Matt 28:20). Disciple-making that teaches a comfortable subset — the encouraging commands, the culturally palatable commands — while quietly omitting the hard commands (self-denial, cross-bearing, sexual purity, costly obedience, the narrow way) is not the disciple-making Christ commanded. The faithful church teaches the whole counsel of God (Acts 20:27), forming apprentices in all that Christ commanded, not in the portions that give no offense.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek mathēteusate (Matt 28:19), the only imperative in the Great Commission; going, baptizing, teaching are the participial means; disciple-making is the formation of baptized apprentices taught to observe all Christ commanded.

expand to see more

Greek mathēteusate (Matt 28:19) — "make disciples," the lone finite imperative of the Great Commission

From mathētēs — a learner-apprentice who follows and is conformed to his master (Luke 6:40)

Modifying participles: poreuthentes (going), baptizontes (baptizing), didaskontes (teaching)

Two halves: baptism (initiatory covenant mark) + teaching to observe all things (lifelong formation)

Usage

"Make disciples — the central command and only imperative of the Great Commission (Matt 28:19)."

"Going, baptizing, and teaching are the means; making disciples is the command."

"Not decisions but disciples; not a comfortable subset but all things whatsoever Christ commanded."
